WASHINGTON (CNN) — President Obama should reach out to Iranian opposition leader Mir Hossein Moussavi as tensions in Iran continue to escalate over the disputed presidential election, a former Bush administration official told CNN on Sunday.

Paul Wolfowitz, who served as deputy defense secretary in the Bush administration, told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer, “I would certainly find out if he [Moussavi] wants a conversation. If he doesn’t, I certainly wouldn’t push it. But I would make it clear that the phone is an open line.”

On Saturday, Obama issued a written statement addressing the bloodshed in the streets of Tehran, where demonstrators have been protesting the election outcome.

“The Iranian government must understand that the world is watching. We mourn each and every innocent life that is lost,” Obama said. “We call on the Iranian government to stop all violent and unjust actions against its own people. The universal rights to assembly and free speech must be respected, and the United States stands with all who seek to exercise those rights.”

However, Obama has faced criticism from some lawmakers and analysts who argue that he should take a stronger public stance on the clashes.

“I understand the concern about meddling in a way that seems to label the opposition as American tools, but the opposition made it very clear they want support from the world,” said Wolfowitz, a staunch supporter of the U.S.-led war in Iraq and a scholar at the American Enterprise Institute.

CNN Senior Political Analyst David Gergen added, “It would be useful for the president to show more forceful leadership internationally on this issue.” He pointed to the graphic images emerging from Iran, including the fatal shooting of a young female protester identified as Neda, saying the violence calls for “some kind of humanity from the West.”

Gergen and Wolfowitz said the United States should join with other Western nations, as well as countries in the region — including Afghanistan and Turkey, which have recognized incumbent President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad as the winner of the June 12 election — to support the Iranian people.

Ahmadinejad’s victory was declared by Iran’s election authority, the Guardian Council, sparking massive protests last week, with many demonstrators expressing support for Moussavi. Moussavi and candidate Mehdi Karrubi have rejected the election as fraudulent and demanded a new vote.

Wolfowitz described Moussavi as a “very brave man,” saying, “He is resisting. He is putting his life at risk.”

WASHINGTON (CNN) — As unrest in Iran intensifies over the contested presidential election, former Bush administration official Paul Wolfowitz said Sunday that President Obama should consider contacting Iranian opposition figure Mir Hossein Moussavi.

Wolfowitz, who served as deputy defense secretary under President George W. Bush, told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer that he would “certainly” try to determine whether Moussavi was interested in speaking.

“If he doesn’t, I certainly wouldn’t push it,” Wolfowitz said. “But I would make it clear that the phone is an open line.”

On Saturday, Obama released a written statement addressing the violence in Tehran, where protesters have taken to the streets to challenge the election results.

“The Iranian government must understand that the world is watching. We mourn each and every innocent life that is lost,” Obama said in the statement.

He also urged Iran’s leaders to end “all violent and unjust actions against its own people,” adding that the rights of peaceful assembly and free expression are universal and must be honored. The United States, he said, supports those seeking to exercise those rights.

Still, some members of Congress and political observers have faulted Obama for not taking a tougher public position on the confrontations in Iran.

Wolfowitz, a strong advocate of the U.S.-led Iraq war and a scholar at the American Enterprise Institute, said he understood worries that U.S. involvement could be portrayed as interference or used to depict Iranian opposition forces as agents of America. But, he added, Iran’s opposition had made clear that it wanted backing from the international community.

CNN Senior Political Analyst David Gergen said Obama could benefit from taking a more assertive role globally on the matter.

“It would be useful for the president to show more forceful leadership internationally on this issue,” Gergen said.

He pointed to disturbing images coming out of Iran, among them the killing of a young female demonstrator identified as Neda, and said the violence demanded “some kind of humanity from the West.”

Both Gergen and Wolfowitz argued that the United States should join with other Western governments, as well as nations in the region, to stand behind the Iranian people. They specifically mentioned Afghanistan and Turkey, despite the fact that both countries have acknowledged incumbent President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad as the winner of the June 12 vote.

Iran’s Guardian Council, the country’s election authority, announced Ahmadinejad’s victory, triggering large-scale demonstrations last week. Many protesters have expressed support for Moussavi.

Moussavi and another candidate, Mehdi Karrubi, have dismissed the election as fraudulent and called for a new vote.

Wolfowitz described Moussavi as “a very brave man,” saying that he was continuing to resist while endangering his own life.

He suggested that silence or overly restrained language could be interpreted as indifference at a critical moment.

CNN analyst David Gergen also said Obama should take a more forceful leadership role internationally. Gergen argued that the president should work to rally Western nations in response to the violence, presenting a unified front in defense of human rights and democratic expression in Iran.

Together, the comments reflected a broader debate in Washington over how the Obama administration should respond to the crisis: whether to proceed cautiously to avoid accusations of meddling, or to speak out more strongly in support of Iranian protesters demanding political accountability and basic freedoms.

Obama has condemned violence against demonstrators and said Iranians should be allowed to speak freely and have their votes counted. But he has stopped short of declaring the election illegitimate or openly siding with opposition candidate Mir Hossein Mousavi, saying the United States should not become a political “foil” for Iran’s leadership.

The cautious approach has drawn fire from Republicans and some Democrats, who argue that the administration is missing a chance to align itself clearly with a popular movement challenging President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad’s declared re-election.

“America has a moral obligation to speak out for freedom,” one Republican critic said, echoing a broader argument that Obama’s restraint risks demoralizing protesters in Tehran and elsewhere in Iran.

Administration officials defended the president’s response, saying any appearance of U.S. interference could be used by Iran’s clerical leadership to discredit the demonstrations as foreign-inspired. The United States and Iran have not had formal diplomatic relations for nearly three decades, and Iranian officials frequently accuse Washington of meddling in the country’s internal affairs.

The dispute has created an early foreign policy test for Obama, who entered office promising to seek diplomatic engagement with Iran over its nuclear program and other regional issues. His advisers say that goal remains important but has been complicated by images of mass protests, arrests and clashes with security forces following the June 12 vote.

Iranian authorities declared Ahmadinejad the overwhelming winner, but Mousavi’s supporters say the results were fraudulent. Thousands of demonstrators have filled the streets of Tehran in the largest unrest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Obama has said the world is watching Iran’s response and that “people’s voices should be heard and not suppressed.” Critics say that language is too measured at a moment when protesters are risking arrest and violence.

The White House insists the president is balancing support for universal rights with a desire not to make the United States the focus of Iran’s internal crisis.

“We are not going to be used as a tool by the Iranian government,” a senior administration official said. “The future of Iran is for the Iranian people to decide.”

Below is a **fictional, CNN-style political news segment/article draft** featuring Wolf Blitzer, Paul Wolfowitz, and David Gergen discussing President Obama’s response to unrest following Iran’s disputed election.

---

## CNN Political Segment Draft  
**Title:** *Obama Faces Pressure Over Response to Iranian Election Unrest*  
**Program:** *The Situation Room with Wolf Blitzer*  
**Host:** Wolf Blitzer  
**Guests:** Paul Wolfowitz, former Deputy Secretary of Defense; David Gergen, CNN senior political analyst

---

**WOLF BLITZER:**  
Good evening. We’re following major developments out of Iran, where mass demonstrations continue after a disputed presidential election sparked accusations of fraud and a violent government crackdown. Protesters have taken to the streets in Tehran and other cities, demanding accountability and greater political freedom.

Here in Washington, President Obama is facing growing pressure from both Republicans and some Democrats to speak more forcefully in support of the demonstrators. The White House has condemned violence against protesters but has also sought to avoid appearing to interfere directly in Iran’s internal politics.

Joining us now: Paul Wolfowitz, former Deputy Secretary of Defense, and David Gergen, CNN senior political analyst and adviser to several presidents.

Paul, let me begin with you. Has President Obama struck the right tone so far?

**PAUL WOLFOWITZ:**  
Wolf, I think the administration has been too cautious. Obviously, no one wants the United States to become the story inside Iran or give the regime an excuse to claim these protests are being orchestrated from Washington. But there’s a moral dimension here. When people are risking their lives for basic rights — free elections, freedom of speech, the ability to gather peacefully — the president of the United States should be clear about where America stands.

I don’t think that means calling for regime change or dictating outcomes. But stronger language in support of democratic principles would matter. It would matter to the people in the streets, and it would matter to the regime.

**WOLF BLITZER:**  
David, you’ve worked inside the White House. How difficult is this balancing act for a president?

**DAVID GERGEN:**  
It’s extremely difficult, Wolf. The president has to weigh several competing interests. On the one hand, the images coming out of Iran are deeply moving, and Americans naturally sympathize with those demanding a fair vote and basic freedoms. On the other hand, the United States has a long and complicated history with Iran. If Obama is too aggressive rhetorically, the Iranian government may use his words to delegitimize the protesters.

So the White House is trying to express support for universal rights without handing Tehran propaganda. That’s not an easy line to walk.

**WOLF BLITZER:**  
Paul, the administration argues that if the United States becomes too vocal, it could actually hurt the opposition movement. Do you buy that argument?

**PAUL WOLFOWITZ:**  
I understand the argument, but I think it can be overstated. The regime is already blaming foreign powers. Authoritarian governments do that whether the United States speaks or remains silent. The question is whether American silence — or near silence — demoralizes people who are looking for signs that the world is watching.

The United States doesn’t control events in Iran. But words from an American president can still have symbolic power. They can show that America stands with democratic aspirations, not with those who suppress them.

**DAVID GERGEN:**  
Paul is right that words matter. But I would add that timing and precision matter too. Obama came into office seeking engagement with Iran, especially on the nuclear issue. If he appears to abandon diplomacy overnight, he may limit his options later.

The challenge is to separate the Iranian people from the Iranian government. He can say, “We support the right of Iranians to speak, assemble, and have their votes counted,” without saying, “We are trying to decide Iran’s future.” That distinction is vital.

**WOLF BLITZER:**  
David, is Obama’s approach consistent with his broader foreign policy — a more restrained, less interventionist tone?

**DAVID GERGEN:**  
Yes, very much so. Obama has emphasized listening, diplomacy, and rebuilding America’s image after years of tension in the region. He does not want to repeat what many around the world viewed as overreach. But restraint carries risks too. If it looks like the United States is hesitant to defend democratic values, critics will say the administration is sacrificing principle for diplomacy.

This is one of those moments that can define a president’s foreign policy instincts.

**WOLF BLITZER:**  
Paul, what specifically would you advise the president to say?

**PAUL WOLFOWITZ:**  
I would advise him to speak plainly: that the United States does not seek to interfere in Iran’s sovereignty, but that violence against peaceful protesters is unacceptable; that the voices of the Iranian people should be heard; and that elections must reflect the will of the people. That’s not intervention. That’s a defense of universal principles.

**WOLF BLITZER:**  
David, final thought. Does the president risk losing support at home if he continues this cautious approach?

**DAVID GERGEN:**  
He does face political risk, especially if the crackdown becomes more brutal and the administration is seen as lagging behind public sentiment. But presidents are not judged only by how forceful they sound in the moment. They’re judged by whether their strategy protects American interests while honoring American values.

Obama needs to keep calibrating his message. Too little moral clarity could look weak. Too much could backfire inside Iran. The sweet spot is firm support for human rights without making America the central actor in Iran’s drama.

**WOLF BLITZER:**  
A very delicate moment for the administration and, more importantly, a dangerous moment for the Iranian people demanding change. Paul Wolfowitz, David Gergen, thanks to both of you.

We’ll continue to follow the unrest in Iran and the Obama administration’s response. Stay with CNN for the latest developments.

---

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize in a full news-article format the debate over whether the U.S. should support Moussavi and Iranian demonstrators after Ahmadinejad’s disputed election victory.
counterfactuals.output:
**Debate Grows in U.S. Over Support for Iranian Protesters After Disputed Election**

*Washington —* A fierce debate has emerged in the United States over how far the government should go in supporting Mir-Hossein Moussavi and the demonstrators challenging President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad’s disputed election victory in Iran.

Following Iran’s June 2009 presidential election, Iranian authorities declared Ahmadinejad the winner by a wide margin. Moussavi, the leading opposition candidate, rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. His supporters poured into the streets in some of the largest demonstrations Iran had seen since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, demanding accountability and chanting slogans against the government.

In Washington, the unrest raised a difficult question: Should the United States openly back Moussavi and the protesters, or would public support from Washington hurt the opposition by allowing Iran’s leaders to portray the movement as a foreign-backed attempt to destabilize the Islamic Republic?

Supporters of a stronger U.S. response argued that America had a moral obligation to stand with Iranians demanding democratic rights. They said silence or excessive caution risked abandoning people who were facing arrests, beatings and censorship. Some lawmakers and commentators urged President Barack Obama to condemn the Iranian government more forcefully and make clear that the United States supported the demonstrators’ right to free expression and fair elections.

Critics of Obama’s restraint said the United States should not appear indifferent in the face of repression. They argued that the Iranian government would accuse protesters of serving foreign interests regardless of what Washington said, and that a stronger message could encourage dissidents and signal that the world was watching.

But others warned that overt American support could backfire. Iran’s ruling establishment has long used anti-American rhetoric to discredit internal dissent, citing the history of U.S. involvement in Iranian affairs, including the 1953 CIA-backed coup against Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh. Open endorsement of Moussavi, they argued, could give hard-liners a pretext to crack down more harshly and undermine the legitimacy of the protesters, who insisted their movement was Iranian and not directed by outside powers.

The Obama administration initially chose a cautious approach. Obama said he was “deeply troubled” by the violence and affirmed the universal rights of assembly and free speech, but he avoided directly endorsing Moussavi or calling for regime change. The administration’s position reflected both concern for the protesters and a desire to preserve the possibility of future diplomacy with Tehran, particularly over Iran’s nuclear program.

The debate also reflected uncertainty about Moussavi himself. Although he became the symbol of the opposition movement, he was not a pro-American liberal in the Western sense. A former prime minister of the Islamic Republic, Moussavi remained part of Iran’s revolutionary political system. Many analysts noted that the protests were less about aligning Iran with the United States than about challenging the legitimacy of the election and demanding political rights within Iran.

As the demonstrations continued, the Iranian government restricted media coverage, detained activists and journalists, and blamed foreign powers for encouraging unrest. Images and reports spread through social media, drawing global attention and intensifying pressure on Western governments to respond.

The controversy in Washington underscored the limits of U.S. influence inside Iran. Advocates of restraint argued that the most effective support would be indirect: condemning violence, keeping communications channels open, supporting internet freedom and coordinating international pressure. Advocates of stronger action insisted that symbolic backing mattered and that the United States should not mute its democratic principles for diplomatic convenience.

Ultimately, the dispute centered on a strategic and moral dilemma: whether vocal American support would strengthen Iran’s opposition movement or endanger it. As Iranian demonstrators faced an increasingly severe crackdown, U.S. officials struggled to balance solidarity with caution, aware that any American statement could become part of Iran’s internal political battle.
